nodes.summary: Front matter of a Court of Inquiry Record of Proceedings (Volume I of 2, Unclassified, pages 1-280), convened at Naval Submarine Base New London, Groton, Connecticut, and Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, Portsmouth, New Hampshire, by order of the Commander in Chief, Atlantic Fleet. title: Unclassified

nodes.title: Unclassified (intro)
nodes.summary: Findings of a 1963 U.S. Navy Court of Inquiry into the loss of the nuclear attack submarine USS Thresher (SSN-593) on 10 April 1963 with all aboard. Covers the crew and shipyard/contractor personnel list, the sea trial and escort by USS Skylark, the final underwater communications, the search (including Recovery, Seawolf, debris and oil slick, no radiation or sabotage found), and command notifications. Also covers design, construction and testing history, HY-80 steel and silver-braze joint quality problems, flooding and high-pressure air blow limits, auxiliary seawater and electrical vulnerabilities, shock-test damage, the lengthy post-shakedown availability, and documentation gaps.

nodes.title: Unclassified
Unclassified (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from the THRESHER (SSN-593) Court of Inquiry findings covering: high-pressure air/hydraulic system particulate contamination and valve leakage corrected before sea trials; hull repairs checked satisfactory; over-pressurization of Reserve Feed Tank No. 2 on 8 March 1963 displacing the tank top and distiller, repaired but not retested, with later stress analysis finding levels acceptable; incomplete ship documentation; no required damage-control or flooding studies; failed fast cruises and deep-dive sea valve testing omitted; Portsmouth Naval Shipyard issues including quality program growth, rip-out procedure absence, deviation from specs, process non-adherence, and unclean Shop 56; a water-stream demonstration; and prior flooding casualties during builder's trials.

nodes.title: a. THRESHER
nodes.summary: Covers the THRESHER and ETHAN ALLEN submarine builder's trials. Ethan Allen trials saw electrical switchboards sprayed and minor fires when a threaded plug blew out of a trim line priming strainer. In first trials, three grease lines through the after engine room bulkhead carried away, a 1.25-inch nipple in the high-pressure air compressor cooling discharge pulled out of a pipe boss at test depth, and inspection found a leaking silbraze joint in a five-inch line.

nodes.title: c. SNOOK
nodes.summary: Excerpts from a 1960s submarine safety report (Thresher-era) listing flooding and joint/hose failures on submarines (Snook, Argonaut, Caiman, Barbel, Skate, Nautilus). Discusses rising submarine complexity, lack of a single Navy submarine-safety organization, inadequate diver trainer simulation of flooding, a 500-foot depth restriction, shipbuilding budget growth, reduced civilian and engineering-officer staffing, and post-shakedown personnel changes on THRESHER.

Excerpts from the THRESHER (SSN-593) Court of Inquiry: air/hydraulic contamination and valve leaks fixed before sea trials; hull repairs satisfactory; Reserve Feed Tank No. 2 overpressurization (March 1963) repaired, not retested, later deemed acceptable; incomplete documentation; no damage-control or flooding studies; fast cruise and deep-dive sea valve tests omitted; Portsmouth Shipyard quality, procedure, spec-deviation and cleanliness failures; builder's trial flooding and pipe/grease line failures on THRESHER and ETHAN ALLEN; 1960s safety report on submarine flooding and joint failures, complexity, lack of safety organization, diver trainer limits, depth restriction, budget and staffing issues.

summary: Findings of the 1963 U.S. Navy Court of Inquiry into the loss of USS Thresher (SSN-593) on 10 April 1963 with all aboard. Covers crew and contractor personnel, sea trial and Skylark escort, final communications, search and debris (no radiation or sabotage found), notifications, design/construction/testing history, HY-80 steel and silver-braze joint problems, flooding and air blow limits, seawater and electrical vulnerabilities, shock-test damage, post-shakedown delays, documentation gaps, and Portsmouth Shipyard quality failures.

title: OPINIONS
summary: Opinions from a 1963 U.S. Navy investigation into the USS THRESHER's loss. It concludes the loss likely resulted from an initial flooding casualty in the engine room, compounded by loss of reactor power, inadequate operating procedures, and a blow system with low capacity and blow rate prone to freeze-up. Other possible causes include sil-braze joint failures, hull or hose failure, and unknown component failures. Recommendations cover deep-depth sea valve operability, low-pressure auxiliary sea water systems, split-plant operation, closing constant vents, sil-braze joint inspection, shock test limits, and improved shipyard quality assurance at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard.

title: Unclassified

nodes.title: Unclassified (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a 1960s-era submarine (THRESHER-class) review covering: quality assurance gaps (flexible hose QA program, QA lacking power to disqualify workers, welding QA not integrated, condition-sheet analysis for management); Portsmouth Naval Shipyard's inadequate particulate/super-cleanliness practices and training; tagging of dummy/backwards valves; improved Pipe Shop work; type commander hull surveillance evaluation; flexible hose and pipe joint identification programs; Ship Information Books; need for detailed repair, inspection and audit procedures; a Ship's System Status (rip-out) procedure; design-stage coordination with operators and damage control; good THRESHER-class design; and air system design reviews (ballast blow rates, air banks, filtration, drainage, fail-open valves, emergency blow) plus full-blow testing at test depth and equipment placement for damage resistance.

nodes.title: a. b(3) 10 USC 130
nodes.summary: The text is the findings section of the Navy court of inquiry into the 1963 loss of the submarine USS Thresher. It covers: flooding and electrical vulnerabilities in the machinery and engine rooms; inadequate damage-control training simulators; three computer-based scenarios estimating the flooding orifice size (about 2 to 4 inches) and the sequence of events from 0909 to 0918 on April 10, 1963; the Skylark commander's delayed reporting, deemed non-contributory; the Shipyard's manpower loading and crew rest; and personnel shortages at the Bureau of Ships and Portsmouth Naval Shipyard. It concludes that no individual was at fault, but that systemic shortcomings need correction across submarine construction and repair.

summary: Covers a 1960s THRESHER-class submarine review: quality assurance gaps (hose and welding QA, condition-sheet analysis), Portsmouth Shipyard cleanliness and training deficiencies, mis-tagged valves, Pipe Shop improvements, hull surveillance, Ship Information Books, repair/audit procedures, rip-out procedure, design coordination, good THRESHER design, and air system reviews (blow rates, filtration, fail-open valves, full-blow tests, equipment placement). Also the Navy inquiry findings on the 1963 USS Thresher loss: flooding and electrical vulnerabilities, inadequate damage-control simulators, flooding orifice estimates (2-4 inches), the April 10, 1963 event timeline, a non-contributory delayed report, shipyard manpower and crew rest, and staffing shortages. No individual was at fault, but systemic fixes are needed.

title: RECOMMENDATIONS
key_items: c. Tests of the main ballast tank structure to determine
summary: The text is a 1963 U.S. Navy court of inquiry report on the loss of the submarine USS THRESHER. It lists 20 recommendations covering: keeping interim depth restrictions; redesigning seawater systems (low-pressure auxiliary service, remote hydraulic valves, loop operation, eliminating constant vent); THRESHER-specific modifications; sil-braze joint testing and replacement with welds; deferring shock tests; quality assurance and audits at Portsmouth; air system fixes; damage control and equipment placement; switchboard protection; diving trainer upgrades; deep-depth and high-speed operating procedures; and a safety organization. It also includes testimony from Captain Zurcher and Captain Schmidt on the ship's pre-sailing readiness, fast cruise, sailing orders, crew, and the SKYLARK escort.

title: is THRESHER.
key_items: A. This was SKYLARK making the search. That is about where I bowed out of
summary: Transcript of a 1963 Navy court of inquiry on the USS THRESHER loss. Captain testifies that THRESHER operated under Special Notice 9080 (2 April 1963, Exhibit 4), a sea trial agenda with sequenced dive phases, and that he cannot state her underway time. SKYLARK reported losing communications during the first deep dive. Exhibits cover the departure message (Exhibit 5), navigation charts (Exhibits 6 and 10), SKYLARK's position and speed reports (Exhibits 7 and 9), and COMSUBLANT's queries (Exhibit 8). The captain describes diverting SEA WOLF, SUNBIRD, SEA OWL, and RECOVERY, plus destroyers, aircraft from COMFAIRWING Three, and Admiral Ramage's designation as on-scene commander. He details search situation reports, the change of operational control (Exhibits 11 to 14), recovered debris and oil slick samples, and the decision to notify next of kin from the sailing list starting at 1930. Court members question the test escort responsibility and notification timing; the CNO makes a public release at 2000.

Covers: testimony identifying Exhibit 2, the sailing list of naval officers and crew embarked on THRESHER April 9-10, 1963, plus a civilian list from Portsmouth Naval Shipyard; a witness describing second next-of-kin notifications on the 10th that survivors were unlikely; a Commander (Chief Staff Officer, ComSubDevGroup Two) testifying that Exhibit 15, the Portsmouth civilian list, was received with the ship's sailing list and matches Exhibit 2's civilian names; Exhibit 15 admitted without objection; no further witnesses; recess until 1000 on 12 April.

title: SECOND DAY
summary: Second day of a U.S. Naval Submarine Base New London (Groton, CT) court session on Friday, April 12, 1963. The court convened at 1000 with all prior-present persons returning. A reporter was introduced and sworn in. The court was cleared at 1002 and reopened at 1135. The president announced adjournment to meet at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, Portsmouth, New Hampshire, as soon as practicable. The court adjourned at 1140. Page 17.

title: THIRD DAY

nodes.title: THIRD DAY (intro)
nodes.summary: Transcript of the third day of a 1963 Portsmouth Naval Shipyard court proceeding in which Commander Dean L. Axene, former commanding officer of USS THRESHER, testifies. He covers his naval career, THRESHER's construction, commissioning (August 1961), and sea trials, including an aborted first deep dive caused by faulty instrumentation and a later successful dive to test depth. He describes Board of Inspection and Survey trials, shakedown cruises, SUBROC and special trials, fleet exercises, an operational readiness inspection rated Excellent, an ASW Council demonstration, a tugboat collision at Cape Canaveral with hull repair at Electric Boat, shock trials, and a deliberately extended pre-post-shakedown operating period. He concludes THRESHER was an outstanding submarine, though it had deficiencies later corrected.

nodes.title: A. Without question.
A. Without question. (intro)
nodes.summary: Commander Axene's testimony on USS THRESHER: post-shakedown availability work included replacing the hydraulic fluid Cellulube with petroleum-based oil (a major teardown because gaskets were incompatible), and installing a new experimental sonar that was the controlling job for completion; noise-quieting work was classified. He speculates the loss was a rapid, rather gross flooding casualty giving no time to signal distress, possibly compounding casualties. He was relieved of command on 18 January; about 80 percent of the officers and crew from his tenure remained aboard, and he praised the crew as outstanding. Court questions covered strain-gauge instrumentation, which was installed before and after launch, was redundant, and was tested under David Taylor Model Basin technical direction.

nodes.title: Model
nodes.summary: Testimony about the Shipyard-built ship's design and construction. The witness held pre-launch discussions with Shipyard technical staff, obtained about a hundred minor design changes during roughly a year of construction, and found the design adequate. He judged workmanship good despite Shipyard inefficiency. A court member then asked about the SKYLARK-THRESHER communications: SKYLARK communicated reliably with THRESHER during descent until THRESHER reported approaching test depth, after which nothing more was heard.

nodes.title: A. Yes.
nodes.summary: Transcript of a 1963 USS THRESHER inquiry. Commander Axene testifies that the shipyard's design was adequate, with about a hundred minor design changes made during construction, and that the ship was well built and operated normally, steaming over 30,000 miles in her first year. He describes a tug-caused hole in the ballast tank that did not reach the pressure hull, and explains his deep-dive flooding concerns and the greater danger of end-compartment flooding. He compares THRESHER's crew favorably with NAUTILUS's, says the loss has not reduced his confidence in submarines, and discusses SUBROC carriage (only dummies carried). Lieutenant Watson, navigator of the SKYLARK, then testifies about its position, course, and speed on 10 April 1963, the UQC communications log (Exhibit 16), clock accuracy, and the GERTRUDE check procedure during THRESHER's deep dive.

Commander Axene's USS THRESHER testimony: post-shakedown work replaced Cellulube hydraulic fluid with petroleum oil (gasket incompatibility, major teardown) and installed a controlling experimental sonar; noise work classified. He speculates on rapid gross flooding leaving no distress time, relieved 18 January, ~80% crew retained, praised crew. Strain-gauge instrumentation (redundant, DTMB-directed) covered. Shipyard design adequate with ~100 minor changes, good workmanship. SKYLARK reliably tracked THRESHER until it reported approaching test depth, then silence.

nodes.summary: A 1963 Navy court of inquiry transcript recounting the USS THRESHER's final communications with the escort ship SKYLARK on 13 April 1963. It covers timed UQC/GERTRUDE messages from 0747 to 0932, including depth and course reports, the 0912 'positive up angle, attempting to blow up' message, air-blowing sounds, the garbled 'test depth' transmission at 0917, and a possible hull-breakup noise. It also covers subsequent efforts to reach the submarine (radio checks, QUEBEC, grenade signals, SUBSAFE initiation), the oil slick found later, recovered debris exhibits, LORAN navigation accuracy, and questions from the court and president about timing and bearings.

summary: Section THIRD DAY is a 1963 Portsmouth Naval Shipyard court transcript of Cmdr. Dean L. Axene, ex-CO of USS THRESHER: naval career, construction, 1961 commissioning, sea trials (aborted first deep dive, successful test-depth dive), Board of Inspection trials, SUBROC, fleet exercises, Excellent readiness rating, tugboat collision and repair, shock trials. Post-shakedown work replaced Cellulube with petroleum oil and installed experimental sonar; flooding speculation, crew praise, strain-gauge and design review. SKYLARK tracked THRESHER until silence near test depth. Also covers final 13 April 1963 UQC/GERTRUDE messages, 'attempting to blow up' report, garbled transmission, search efforts, oil slick, debris, LORAN accuracy.

title: REDIRECT EXAMINATION

nodes.title: REDIRECT EXAMINATION (intro)
nodes.summary: Redirect examination of a Navy witness in the USS THRESHER inquiry (April 1963). Covers a radio log discrepancy ('hold you' vs 'to' THRESHER) and a 0917 garbled transmission, with the witness's theory it contained 'exceeding' before 'test depth'. Also covers LORAN fixes (about 65 degrees apart), bottom contours and fathometer soundings, and the witness's navigator tenure since 1962. Then a recess and reconvening, and the testimony of BM3 Roy S. Mowen Jr., UQC operator on USS SKYLARK: the UQC worked well with no identifiable THRESHER noise, a 7-8 thousand yard range, and no reception from a submarine with stern aspect or headway.

nodes.title: A. The Captain, the OD,
nodes.summary: Transcript of a 1963 Navy Court of Inquiry into the loss of USS THRESHER. Testimony covers the UQC (underwater telephone) log of USS SKYLARK on 10 April, including range checks, the garbled and distorted final transmissions ("experiencing minor difficulties, have positive up angle, attempting to blow"; a garbled call ending in "test depth"), a possible tank-blow sound, reception quality, and log-reading procedures. Family members (Joseph Shafer, David Main) describe THRESHER crew concerns about piping and reject rates. Captain Donald Kern, Bureau of Ships, testifies that the hull would be totally flooded at about 8,400 feet, that debris could surface, and that debris alone does not establish the cause of sinking.

summary: Redirect examination of a Navy witness in the April 1963 USS THRESHER inquiry: a radio log discrepancy ('hold you' vs 'to' THRESHER), a garbled 0917 transmission with a possible 'exceeding' before 'test depth', LORAN fixes about 65 degrees apart, bottom contours and fathometer soundings, and the witness's navigator tenure since 1962. After a recess, BM3 Roy S. Mowen Jr., UQC operator on USS SKYLARK, testifies the UQC worked well with no identifiable THRESHER noise, at a 7-8 thousand yard range, and got no reception from a submarine with stern aspect or headway. Also covers a 1963 inquiry's UQC log, garbled final transmissions, a possible tank-blow sound, and family testimony on piping and reject rates. Captain Donald Kern says the hull would flood totally at about 8,400 feet and that debris alone does not establish the cause.

title: EXAMINATION BY THE COURT

nodes.title: EXAMINATION BY THE COURT (intro)
nodes.summary: Court examination transcript of a submarine casualty inquiry. CAPT Nash asks whether the cause of the submarine exceeding collapse/test depth is known; the witness says no, only speculation is possible. Lt. Jack Sousae, DEPCOMSUBLANT staff, testifies on custody of evidence: objects received via USOS Roberts from USOS Skylark, who recovered them from the surface. Exhibits 22-29 are introduced (bottles, drinking glasses, rubber gloves, a plastic tube). Sousae says containers came from Skylark and only contents were found; he checked the plastic-bagged material for radioactivity and found it clear. Frederick L. Downs is then sworn in and begins direct examination.

nodes.title: Questions
nodes.summary: Transcript of a Navy court of inquiry on the USS Thresher loss. Rubber technologist Frederick L. Downs testifies about his background and lab tests on exhibits 19-29: a brown microballoon plastic matching Thresher material, polyurethane foam, cork, borated polyethylene, neoprene glove and foam, and a Polaroid part. John E. Carrigan reports oil and sea water residue, iron-rich material, and borated polyethylene tests. Anthony Faskianos is introduced as the next witness, with testimony pending.

nodes.title: A. Yes, sir, I did.
nodes.summary: Testimony in a 1963 Portsmouth Naval Shipyard inquiry: radiological expert Faskianos tested exhibits with Beta Gamma and Alpha instruments, finding only background readings and no detectable alpha, so no more contamination than ordinary road objects. Court adjourned to Monday 15 April 1963. Lt. Stanley Haecker of USS SKYLARK then testified about its operational readiness inspection, Commander Submarine Flotilla TWO messages and schedule (Exhibits 32-33), and planned coordination with USS THRESHER, including a directive not to mention THRESHER's depth because it was classified.

nodes.title: A. No, sir.
nodes.summary: Testimony excerpt: witness confirms no, then that after getting underway per orders, the vessel SKYLARK proceeded. Questioner asks when that occurred and what SKYLARK did next. Witness offers to read underway and rendezvous times from the Quartermaster's Notebook. Text is OCR-garbled and ends with a note that it is the official Quartermaster's Notebook.

nodes.title: C. f you--r sEip
nodes.summary: Transcript of the Navy Court of Inquiry into the loss of USS THRESHER (April 1963), covering testimony from the SKYLARK's commanding officer and crew on the April 10 events: the rendezvous, the shallow and deep dives, UQC radio logs, the garbled 'attempting to blow' messages, heard air-blowing sounds, search operations, oil slick and debris recovery, and LORAN navigation. Also covers testimony from Portsmouth Shipyard, Submarine Force, and post-shakedown availability officials on sea trial scheduling, readiness, and shipyard work. Further testimony covers the Shipyard's work, crew and training, USS THRESHER debris exhibits, acoustic/SOSUS detections, and a party designation of LCDR Hecker and RADM Palmer.

nodes.title: WITNESS: May
nodes.summary: Transcript excerpt from a naval inquiry hearing on the USS THRESHER loss. A witness (Captain Leehey) testifies about acoustic Exhibits 52-54 recorded by SOSUS stations on 1121-1606 ZULU, including a possible emergency propulsion motor start at 1416 ZULU, lines that terminated abruptly at 1437/1441 ZULU, and his judgment that the signal was 'more likely an ironic coincidence.' Questioning by the President, court members, and counsel covers vessel speed, the bottom-rest time, hull collapse frequencies, and his reasons for doubting his initial conclusion. He declines to classify the acoustic events.

nodes.title: REEXAMINATION BY THE BOARD
nodes.summary: Transcript excerpt from a 1963 Navy board inquiry (Portsmouth Naval Shipyard) on the SOSUS acoustic detection system. Captain Osborn is questioned about detection of the submarine THRESHER and its correlation with FOX; he states detection by southern SOSUS stations is possible but conditions make a valid conclusion doubtful. Witness has no further statements. The president reminds all that SOSUS information is highly classified and notes are to stay in the room. The court adjourns at 2005 hours on 18 April 1963. The seventh day opens on 19 April 1963 with William H. Barnes III called as a civilian witness.

nodes.title: DIRECT EXAMINATION
nodes.summary: Testimony of Marine engineer William H. Barnes III of the U.S. Naval Engineering Experiment Station on his role as BuShips technical director for submarine detection trials, covering structure-borne and radiated noise trials, his background as a submarine officer, and prior THRESHER trials. He states that the exhibit traces (52, 53, 54) show a high probability (about 90 percent) of THRESHER, citing a slight turn pattern near 1210 Zulu that fades around 1250, with nothing contradicting it.

summary: Court of inquiry into the USS Thresher loss (1963). Covers: cause of exceeding test depth unknown; custody of recovered evidence (Exhibits 22-29) and radiological tests finding only background readings; rubber, foam, cork, borated polyethylene and oil/sea-water residue lab results; SKYLARK operations, rendezvous, UQC logs, garbled distress messages and search/debris recovery; SOSUS acoustic exhibits 52-54 analysis, with Leehey and Osborn testimony and classification limits; Barnes assessing about 90 percent probability the signals were Thresher.
